name: Protect Democracy: defending US democracy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends; the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: Protect Democracy litigates, builds tools and coalitions and writes policy to keep the United States from sliding into a more authoritarian government ($34.4 million in 2024). Its year of work is counted as its share of the money behind the US pro-democracy field's work against backsliding (about 1.3%) times the share of the forecast chance of the US leaving the democracies before 2030 (about 11%) that a year of the field's work removes (judged 4.5%); the loss is the income democracy brings (Acemoglu et al. 2019), building over 25 years, put off by the years a win counts and lasting until the slide would be undone (5% a year), and democracy's other goods. A smaller branch counts its work for proportional representation (about a fifth of the result). With its next dollar at 35% of the average that comes to about 0.02 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, about a quarter of the site's global-health median. The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges spanning over ten thousandfold; the biggest is the field's effect on that chance, a judgment with no study behind it. Both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

source.note: $28,277,727, including grants of $7,218,161; one programme described (monitoring, investigating, advocacy, lobbying, public outreach and litigation).

rows.explainer: Everything Protect Democracy Project, the 501(c)(3), spent on its programme in 2024, the latest year with a filed return (the audited statements, which the return says exist, aren't public). Its sister 501(c)(4), Protect Democracy United ($5,532,325 of expenses in 2024, its own Form 990, Part I line 18: https://protectdemocracy.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/FY24-990-PDU-Public-Disclosure-Copy-without-Schedule-B.pdf), is a separate organisation and not in this cost.

rows.label: Total expenses, calendar 2024
rows.explainer: The shared figure from the same return ($34,368,875, Part I line 18), read by the FairVote model too, which divides credit for proportional representation by Protect Democracy's spending.

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programme, calendar 2024
rows.explainer: The whole programme: the return lists one programme, and this model covers all of it, as two branches (defending democracy against backsliding; electoral-system reform). Grants to other organisations ($7.2 million, $5.5 million of it to Amalgamated Charitable Foundation, Schedule I) count as the work they fund, judged to be the same mix as Protect Democracy's own.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over the programme in proportion to its cost.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programme, including overhead
rows.explainer: The year's full cost, the base for the charity's share of the field below.

rows.label: People governed by the US democracy the work defends (2024)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the United States: a slide into a hybrid regime would change how all of them are governed. The chance of that slide and the share of it the work removes are in p_success.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention in the year
rows.explainer: 0: Protect Democracy does no criminal or immigration casework; its cases are about elections, executive power and the people who run elections.

rows.label: Share of the programme spent on proportional representation
rows.explainer: The shared figure (7%, 3% to 15%), read by the FairVote model too: Protect Democracy lists four areas of work (Protecting Free & Fair Elections; Stopping the Consolidation of Power; Building Pro-Democracy Collective Action; Shaping the Democracy of Tomorrow, its own page); the last includes its work for proportional representation (research, a Democracy Journal symposium with Democracy Fund, a grant to Fix Our House) and its AI for Democracy Action Lab, which is counted in the backsliding branch; the return gives no split. The rest is the backsliding branch.

rows.label: Share of the programme spent defending against backsliding
rows.explainer: Litigation (election subversion, defamation suits for election workers, executive overreach), election protection (VoteShield, the National Task Force on Election Crises, the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections), state laws for election officials, the Civil Service Archive and OpenOMB, the AI for Democracy Action Lab, and public education: all aimed at keeping the US from sliding into a more authoritarian government.

rows.label: Chance the US stops being a democracy before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (about 11%): the stake the backsliding work acts on.

rows.label: Share of that chance a year of the US pro-democracy field's work removes
rows.explainer: The whole field's year of litigation, election protection, policy and public education (about $3 billion a year from foundations alone, @democracy.us_democracy_philanthropy_per_year) against a world without it. No study measures this; judged 4.5% (0.5% to 20%), the geometric middle of a lower anchor of about 1% and the range's high of 20%. From below: once autocratization begins, only one in five democracies manage to avert breakdown (Boese et al. 2021, Democratization 28(5), abstract: 36 breakdowns in 59 episodes since 1993, the rest including episodes still under way), so resistance as a whole (courts, elections, officials, the press, civil society) cuts breakdown by about a fifth; durable judicial constraints and long democratic histories are what let democracies prevail, and the field works largely through the courts and election officials. With organised civil society a fifth to a third of that resistance and a year one of five in the window, a year of the field removes 0.8% to 1.3%; the low end is half that. From above: the catastrophic-risk family's typical cut for nuclear-security work, 0.036% of the risk per $1 million (@catastrophe.nuclear_catastrophe_cut_per_million), would give over 100% at the field's $3-4 billion; 4.5% is about a twentieth of that per dollar, for a field a hundred times larger with steeply falling returns, and the high end of 20% a fifth of it. Resources also explain less than 5% of which side wins on contested US policy issues (Baumgartner et al. 2009, @democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate's source). A cut in a chance is counted at its expected value, as the catastrophic-risk family does: the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet, so this isn't a single event.

rows.label: Chance of backsliding removed by a year of the field's work
rows.explainer: The forecast chance times the share the field removes; Protect Democracy's part of it is its share of the field's resources (bs_attribution_share).

rows.label: Years until most of democracy's income effect is realized
rows.explainer: The shared figure (about 25 years, 20 to 30): the income effect of a change in how a country is governed builds up over this long.

rows.label: Income kept per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: A slide out of democracy averted keeps the income gain a democracy brings in the long run (about 21%, Acemoglu et al. 2019); the build-up is in bs_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the year's work until the slide it helps avert would have happened
rows.explainer: The forecast counts the Economist's reports published before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so the window left covers 2026 to 2028, and a slide averted would on average have come in its middle, 2027: three years after 2024's work (2 to 5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (backsliding branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): a slide averted counts as put off by these years, as a won reform counts as brought forward by them.

rows.label: Chance per year that a slide, once it has happened, is undone
rows.explainer: Most recent slides are reversed: '52% of all autocratization episodes become U-Turns, which increases to 73% when focusing on the last 30 years', and 90% of U-turns restore democracy (Nord et al. 2025, When autocratization is reversed: episodes of U-Turns since 1900, Democratization, doi 10.1080/13510347.2024.2448742, abstract). A 5% yearly hazard undoes about 70% of slides within 25 years; judged lower than the 73% because a breakdown to a hybrid regime, the forecast's stake, is harder to undo than an episode stopped earlier (2% to 10%). The loss is treated as ending at reversal, a slight understatement since income recovers at the ramp's pace.

rows.label: Discount rate plus reversal hazard (backsliding branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the chance a slide is undone each year: the loss averted lasts only while the slide would have lasted.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years an averted slide counts (the loss ramp put off)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + bs_rate) * ln(1 + bs_rate) * ramp_years) * bs_wait_discount
rows.explainer: A slide's income loss builds evenly over ramp_years from when it happens; putting the slide off by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp later, so the loss avoided each year is the ramp now minus the ramp years_of_impact later: it rises to a fifth of the full loss (5 of 25 years) over the first five years, stays there until the ramp is complete and falls back to nothing five years later, years_of_impact full-effect years in all before discounting. This is its present value (continuous form) at the shared rate plus the chance the slide would be undone (bs_rate), times the wait (at the shared rate): at the defaults about 1.5 full-effect years (5 undiscounted). Whether the slide comes later anyway is the question years_of_impact answers; how long it would last is bs_reversal_rate's.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the field's work (backsliding branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the US × the long-run income kept × the shared value of a log point × the chance removed × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: People newly governed under proportional representation per year of the movement's work
rows.explainer: The shared figure, read by the FairVote model too: proportional representation in the US is won city by city for now (Portland, Oregon, about 650,000 people, in November 2022); about 230,000 people a year of the whole movement's work in expectation (50,000 to 2 million).

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a switch to proportional representation brings
rows.explainer: The shared figure (5%, 1% to 15%), read by the FairVote model too: a reform within a democracy gets a ranged share of the democratization gain, never the whole (the family's rule); no study finds a robust income effect of proportional representation in rich democracies.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The reform's share of the long-run democratization gain; the build-up is in ref_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the win until the new system is first used
rows.explainer: The shared figure: two years (1 to 4), as in Portland (voted November 2022, first used November 2024).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the shared yearly chance a won electoral reform is repealed (@democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate, 3%): repeal is a separate question from the years counted (the family's rule).

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won reform counts (its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + ref_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + ref_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + ref_rate) * ln(1 + ref_rate) * ramp_years) * ref_wait_discount
rows.explainer: As for the backsliding branch: the reform's effect builds over ramp_years from adoption, and bringing adoption forward by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp earlier; present value at the shared rate plus the repeal hazard, times the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the movement's work (reform branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly covered (already an expected count, so no separate chance) × the income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Income kept per person affected per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: The backsliding branch's figure, for reading: the main channel.

rows.label: Share of the full democracy-to-autocracy loss a slide to a hybrid regime brings
rows.explainer: Acemoglu et al. code a country as democratic or not; the forecast is of a slide to the Economist's 'hybrid regime' (elections held but not free or fair), short of the full autocracy their estimate compares with. Judged 60% (30% to 100%): Hungary and Turkey, the nearest cases, kept elections and markets but lost courts' and the press's independence.

rows.label: Validity of the cross-country income effect for the United States
rows.explainer: The estimate comes from 175 countries, most of them poorer than the US, where democracy raised growth through investment, schooling and reforms that a rich country already has; a rich country's private institutions may hold up more of its income. Judged 0.8 (0.5 to 1).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, backsliding branch
rows.explainer: The two parts above: how much of the cross-country effect a US slide would bring.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, reform branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure (0.6, 0.3 to 0.9), read by the FairVote model too: the doubt that proportional representation in US cities changes outcomes at all (few cases, first used in 2024); above the backsliding branch's 0.48 only because it measures a different doubt.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway, backsliding branch
rows.explainer: 1: the field's risk cut is already measured against a world without the field's work (others' actions, courts and voters are the baseline), and Protect Democracy's part is its share of the field's resources below, so nothing more is subtracted.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway, reform branch
rows.explainer: 1: the people covered are the movement's expected wins, and $win_years_counted already says they would have come some day.

rows.label: The whole field's money as a multiple of institutional 501(c)(3) philanthropy
rows.explainer: The shared figure counts only institutional philanthropy to 501(c)(3) work in 2021-2022, but the risk cut is the whole field's. Democracy Fund's own report says 501(c)(4) funding would raise its 2021-2022 total from $6.9 to $7.8 billion (+13%, p. 16, note 10), that individual donors are left out and the field's overall size would be larger (p. 15), and that 45% of funders planned to give more in 2023-2024 against 8% less (p. 3); law firms' pro bono work comes on top. Against that, the report names biases the other way: survey response from growing funders and a broader taxonomy than Candid's (p. 15), and slower individual giving in 2023-2024 (p. 16). Judged 1.5 (1.2 to 2.2): ×1.13 for 501(c)(4)s, about ×1.15 for real growth to 2024 and ×1.15 for individual donors and pro bono, the range covering both directions.

rows.label: Share of US democracy money spent on work acting on backsliding as directly as Protect Democracy's
rows.explainer: Democracy Fund's total covers elections and voting, the rule of law and accountability, civic engagement and education, money in politics and the information ecosystem. Protect Democracy's kind of work (litigation, election protection, checks on executive power, election-official support) is part of it. Judged 40% (20% to 70%).

rows.label: Effect on backsliding of a dollar of the field's other work, against a direct dollar
rows.explainer: The rest of the field (turnout drives, civic education, local news, money in politics) also acts on backsliding, less directly, and so shares in the risk cut. Judged a fifth of a direct dollar's effect (0 to half).

rows.label: Resources behind the field's work against backsliding, in direct-work dollars of 2024
rows.explainer: Institutional philanthropy for democracy (2021-2022) × the whole field's money against it × the direct share plus the rest at its relative effect, in 2024 prices: the field whose year of work the risk cut belongs to.

rows.label: Protect Democracy's share of the field's resources, backsliding branch
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on this work over the field's (Convention 2: share of resources, never an equal split): about 1.3%. It applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Protect Democracy's share of the proportional-representation movement's resources
rows.explainer: Its spending on this work over the movement's: its own, FairVote's (its 2024 spending × @democracy.fairvote_pr_share) and the other groups' (@democracy.us_pr_other_resources_per_year); the FairVote model divides by the same three (Convention 2): about 31%.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured, backsliding branch
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step: no count of what the work changed exists, the effect is built from the cross-country literature and judgments.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured, reform branch
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step: the reach is a judgment and the effect is judged.

rows.label: Share of the win that is enforced

rows.label: Side effect: the good of democracy beyond income, as a share of the income value
rows.explainer: Living under a democracy is worth more than its income: freedom of speech and assembly, fair treatment by the state, no fear of arrest for opposing the government. Helliwell and Huang (2008, British Journal of Political Science 38(4)) find that the quality of government is linked to life satisfaction beyond its link through income, and more so in richer countries. Across 165 countries in 2005-2023, autocratization shows no clear overall link with life satisfaction, but a negative one in established democracies on 4 of 8 measures (Autocratization and Subjective Well-Being: Is There a Macro-Level Effect?, Applied Research in Quality of Life, 2026, doi 10.1007/s11482-026-10660-0, abstract), which supports a value beyond income for a rich democracy and the low end of the range. No study gives the size for a slide in a rich democracy; judged 30% of the income value (10% to 100%).

rows.label: Side effect: non-fatal repression and intimidation averted, as a share of the income value
rows.explainer: Autocratizing countries see more state repression: arrests, surveillance, threats against officials, journalists and opponents; Protect Democracy also works directly against intimidation (the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections' 150 trainings with election officials and police in 35 states, its page). Non-fatal harms only, judged 5% of the income value (0 to 20%). Deaths from political violence are left out: US political violence kills tens of people a year, which against 340 million people's incomes and a share of a chance would be under 1% of the result.

rows.label: Side effect: US democracy's effect on democracy abroad, as a share of the income value
rows.explainer: Democracy spreads from neighbours and partners (Boese et al. 2021 find more democratic neighbours help democracies prevail), and a US that left the democracies would weaken that pull worldwide and its support for democrats abroad. Judged 20% of the US income value (0 to 60%).

rows.label: Side effect: backlash and polarization the work provokes
rows.explainer: Litigation and campaigns seen as partisan can harden the other side and invite counter-measures (state bans on ranked-choice voting followed local wins, @democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate's source). Judged −5% (−15% to 0).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not in the main chain, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The two side effects of both branches (democracy's goods beyond income, backlash), each with its sign and weighted by the side-effects slider; the two that belong only to an averted slide enter the backsliding branch through bs_slide_side_factor.

rows.label: Backsliding branch: its slide-only side effects, as a factor
rows.explainer: Repression averted and the pull of US democracy abroad belong to an averted slide, not to proportional representation: this factor adds them to the backsliding branch only, so with outcome_total's (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) the branch counts 1 + all four side effects, the reform branch 1 + the other two.
